title: Crime and Punishment
author: Fyodor Dostoevsky
openingText: On an exceptionally hot evening early in July a young man came out of the garret in which he lodged in S. Place and walked slowly, as though in hesitation, towards K. bridge. He had successfully avoided meeting his landlady on the staircase. His garret was under the roof of a high, five-storied house and was more like a cupboard than a room. The landlady who provided him with garret, dinners, and attendance, lived on the floor below.
about:
Crime and Punishment follows Rodion Romanovitch Raskolnikov, a poor former student in St. Petersburg. He murders an old pawnbroker and her sister, who enters unexpectedly. He has developed a theory that extraordinary people may be entitled to break the law in pursuit of a great idea. The murder gives him neither the freedom nor the certainty about himself that he imagined. Fever, fear, pride and his need for other people pull him in different directions.

Around him are his sister Dounia, his mother Pulcheria Alexandrovna, his friend Razumihin and Sonia, who has turned to prostitution to support her family. The investigator Porfiry tests his explanations and presses him toward confession. The landowner Svidrigaïlov gives the question of freedom without moral limits another disturbing form.

Published in 1866, the novel combines a crime story with an inquiry into conscience, poverty, faith and responsibility. Confession is not the same as repentance, and punishment does not by itself produce transformation. The distance between these things makes its ending worth debating.

angleCards.title: The theory that destroys itself.
angleCards.text: Raskolnikov believes extraordinary people may have the right to exceed ordinary moral law. I want to follow how the murder tests his idea and why he keeps defending it despite his suffering.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow how Raskolnikov defends and questions his theory, even after the murder has brought disastrous consequences.

angleCards.title: Guilt as a physical thing.
angleCards.text: Raskolnikov sweats, hallucinates, collapses and rages. I want to notice how the novel connects his thoughts to bodily reactions, and how difficult it is to distinguish guilt from fear, illness and wounded pride.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Crime and Punishment as a study of guilt as a physical experience — how Dostoevsky makes psychological suffering visible, almost somatic.

angleCards.title: Sonia as the answer.
angleCards.text: Sonia lives in harsh circumstances and meets Raskolnikov with compassion. I want to examine what her faith and insistence on responsibility mean to him, and whether her actions challenge his theory more than her words do.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to read Sonia as the counter-argument to everything Raskolnikov believes — how Dostoevsky uses her as the embodiment of faith against theory.

angleCards.title: Redemption or surrender?
angleCards.text: The confession and the beginning of transformation in the epilogue are separate moments. I want to examine what makes Raskolnikov surrender and whether the ending makes his change convincing.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to distinguish confession, punishment and repentance, and ask what actually changes Raskolnikov.

cast.name: Raskolnikov
cast.description: A poor former law student of twenty-three, living in a tiny room in St. Petersburg. Proud and intelligent, he is also generous, cruel, vulnerable and contradictory. His theory of extraordinary people’s rights is tested by his own actions. The narrative follows him closely but also enters other people’s lives and perspectives.

cast.name: Sonia Marmeladova
cast.description: A young woman who turns to prostitution to support her father, stepmother and the hungry children. Devout and compassionate, she also experiences fear, humiliation and despair. She listens to Raskolnikov’s confession, urges him to accept responsibility and follows him to Siberia.

cast.name: Porfiry Petrovitch
cast.description: An investigator who combines a jovial manner with sharp questions and psychological pressure. He lets Raskolnikov talk, challenges his theory and eventually confronts him directly with his suspicions. Their conversations connect the investigation with the novel’s moral conflict.

cast.name: Dounia
cast.description: Raskolnikov's sister, beautiful and proud. She has agreed to marry the cold and calculating Luzhin to save the family from ruin — a sacrifice her brother cannot bear. Her plotline runs in parallel to his: a different test of moral strength under pressure, a different decision about what one is willing to barter for security. She refuses Luzhin. She survives Svidrigaïlov. She marries the decent Razumihin. She is the novel's quiet counterargument to its hero.

cast.name: Svidrigaïlov
cast.description: A wealthy landowner who pursues Dounia and tries to gain power over her. Rumours of earlier abuse surround him. His cynicism and appetite make him a disturbing counterpart to Raskolnikov, but his actions also include financial help for Sonia and the children. The novel makes him difficult to reduce to a single explanation.

cast.name: Razumihin
cast.description: Raskolnikov’s poor, energetic and loyal friend. He nurses him during his illness, helps his family and falls in love with Dounia. His practical care and willingness to work offer another way through poverty than Raskolnikov’s theory.

acclaim.quote: Dostoiewsky who, incidentally, was the only psychologist from whom I had anything to learn
acclaim.context: Twilight of the Idols, “Skirmishes in a War with the Age” §45; written 1888, published 1889. Anthony M. Ludovici translation. On Dostoevsky generally.

whyItMatters.title: A Close Portrait of a Divided Mind
whyItMatters.body: The novel follows Raskolnikov’s shifts between self-justification, panic, pride and longing for human contact. Readers know the murderer from the start; the suspense also concerns what he will understand about himself. Dreams, fever and conversations turn thought into action. This is a powerful psychological novel, but neither the first of its kind nor a narrative confined entirely to his consciousness.

whyItMatters.title: Who May Break the Law?
whyItMatters.body: Raskolnikov draws on lawgivers, discoverers and conquerors in explaining his theory. He wants to find out whether he belongs among those entitled to exceed ordinary rules. The novel tests that idea against the actual people it turns into instruments. His suffering after the murder cannot simply be equated with repentance: even in prison, he continues to defend his idea.

whyItMatters.title: Sonia, Faith and Responsibility
whyItMatters.body: Sonia reads Raskolnikov the story of Lazarus and asks him to acknowledge his act publicly. Her compassion does not remove the demand for responsibility. The epilogue links her love and faith with the possibility of a new life, but calls his transformation the beginning of another story. Readers must judge how convincing that promise is.
